nameStory: The 'salted shield' name comes from the whitish, granular soredia (tiny reproductive structures) scattered across its surface that look remarkably like coarse salt crystals sprinkled on food. The 'shield' part refers to its flat, leafy growth form that spreads across rock surfaces like overlapping medieval shields. It's also called 'crottle,' an old Scottish name for lichens used to dye wool.
description: Salted Shield Lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms gray-green to bluish-gray patches on rocks and stone walls. It grows in overlapping, leaf-like lobes that create circular or irregular colonies several inches across. The surface has a distinctive frosted appearance from tiny white granules, and the edges of the lobes are often darker. This is one of the classic 'shield lichens' you'll encounter on New England's abundant stone walls and rocky outcrops.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for tiny white granules (soredia) scattered across the surface that feel slightly gritty to the touch, like coarse salt or sugar crystals dusted on top

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leaf-like lobes that overlap each other like roof shingles, creating circular patches that spread outward from the center

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to bluish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; the lobe edges are often noticeably darker than the center

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found on hard surfaces like granite boulders, stone walls, concrete, or acidic rock faces in partial shade

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes are typically 0.5-1 inch wide, but colonies can spread to cover areas 6 inches across or larger on suitable surfaces

habitat: Salted Shield Lichen thrives on acidic rocks throughout New England's forests, from granite outcrops in the White Mountains to the ubiquitous stone walls crisscrossing the region. It prefers partially shaded locations with good air circulation, often growing alongside mosses and other lichens on north-facing or sheltered rock surfaces. You'll commonly spot it on old cemetery headstones, bridge abutments, and the countless fieldstone walls that define New England's rural landscape.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the thallus turns bright green and the white soredia appear especially prominent against the wet surface. Growth resumes slowly after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Appears grayer and more subdued during dry periods, but the distinctive salt-like granules remain visible. Look for it in shaded spots where it stays slightly moist.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture brings out rich colors again, and this is an excellent time to observe the contrast between the gray-green center and darker lobe margins.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under snow and becomes more noticeable when deciduous trees are bare. The texture and white granules are still diagnostic even when colors are muted.

funFact: This humble rock-dweller was once so valuable that Scottish Highlanders fought over the best lichen-gathering territories - they used it to create rich orange, yellow, and red dyes for their clan tartans, with the colors varying depending on which mordants (chemical fixatives) they used with the lichen extract.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Netted Shield Lichen, which has a distinctive net-like pattern of white lines instead of scattered granules. Memory trick: 'Salted' has scattered salt-like granules, while 'Netted' has connected lines forming a net pattern.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'crottle' comes from Scottish Gaelic and refers to several lichen species used for dyeing - if you see this alternate name in field guides, it may refer to different species depending on the region. DNA studies have revealed that what was once considered a single widespread species actually includes several look-alike species that can only be distinguished genetically.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin the Netted Shield Lichen which has raised white ridges forming a net pattern, Salted Shield Lichen has scattered granular patches. Bottlebrush Shield Lichen has distinctive finger-like projections (isidia) rather than granules. The closely related Smoky Crottle tends to be darker overall and typically lacks the prominent white soredia that give Salted Shield its characteristic 'salted' appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Netted shield lichen is distinguished from its shield lichen relatives by its unique white net pattern - bottlebrush shield lichen has tiny finger-like projections, while salted shield lichen has a more uniformly smooth surface with white spots rather than a connected network.

Bottlebrush shield lichen stands out from other Parmelia species by its distinctive branching edge projections - netted shield lichen has a more reticulated (net-like) surface pattern, while salted shield lichen has simpler, less ornate edges.

Unlike Netted Shield Lichen which has a distinctly white, net-like pattern on its surface, or Bottlebrush Shield Lichen with its fuzzy, hair-like projections, Smoky Crottle has a relatively smooth surface.
Among the shield lichens, fertile shield lichen is distinguished by its pale, prominent pores and frequent fruiting body production.
